**Which restart command to use:**

| What changed | Command | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `app/**/*.py`, `assets/*.css`, `app/ui/*.py`, SQL queries | `restart app worker` | Bind-mount means code on disk is what containers run; a restart re-reads everything in the existing container. Fast (~30s including Reflex recompile). |
| New `pyproject.toml` dep, app `Dockerfile` change | `up -d --build worker app` | Need a fresh image. |
| `docker/postgres/Dockerfile` change (pgvector / base image) | `up -d --build postgres` — **then read [Postgres image and collation parity](#postgres-image-and-collation-parity) before running it** | The `postgres` service is a *build*, not a pull, so `--build postgres` is required or the DB keeps its old image. Changing its base OS is a collation event, not a routine rebuild. |
| `.env` change, `docker-compose*.yml` change, Celery beat schedule change | `up -d --force-recreate worker app` | Restart doesn't re-read `env_file` or the resolved compose config. Force-recreate does. Critical when a beat schedule changes (Celery beat config only loads at container create, not on `restart`). |
| Alembic migration added | Run migration **before** restart, in a one-shot `app` container: `sudo docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml run --rm app python -m alembic upgrade head` then `restart` as above. | Migration is idempotent — the running `app` also runs `alembic upgrade head` at startup, but doing it explicitly first surfaces errors before the new code is serving. |

## Postgres image and collation parity

The `postgres` service is built from `docker/postgres/Dockerfile`, which starts
from **`postgres:16-bookworm`** (an explicitly pinned OS release, never the
floating `postgres:16` tag) and adds pgvector. Any future Postgres image change

### Managing tenant access (who belongs to which tenant)

**The console is the sanctioned path.** Sign in as a system admin → **Tenants** → **Members**
on the account's row. The drawer lists current members and does the whole workflow: add an
existing user, change someone's role between Admin and Read only, and remove access. Every
one of those writes goes through the audited admin plane and lands a durable `audit_logs`
row attributed to you — which the raw SQL it replaces never did.

Adding someone: type their email → **Find** → confirm the account shown → pick a role →
**Add to this account**. Three outcomes are normal, not errors:

| What you see | What it means |
|---|---|
| "No user with this email has logged in yet" | The person has no account. Users exist only after a first IdP login, so there is nothing to grant. Have them sign in once (or use `seed-tenant-admin` above if the tenant is new too), then come back. |
| Two or more accounts on one email | Two IdP subjects can legitimately share an address. Pick the right one — the console never guesses, because no write path may dereference an email. |
| "already a member with a different role" | The grant was refused on purpose. Use the role control on their row instead; a role change hiding inside an "add" is a write the audit trail would misdescribe. |

Re-adding someone who already has the same role is safe and does nothing — repeat grants are
idempotent by design.

later OIDC login that still carries `tenant_slug` for that account will **not** mint it again.

users are granted through this console or the API below. If they still belong to another tenant,
that remaining membership is what the session binds.

`is_active` are owned by Keycloak and re-derived at **every** login, so a write here would
silently revert. Change those in Keycloak. Membership roles are the only axis this manages.

### Audit what a Klaviyo API key can actually do

Klaviyo has **no supported endpoint for reading a key's scopes** (`GET /api-keys/` is beta and
404s at revision `2024-10-15`), and **scopes are immutable after creation** — every scope change
is a full key rotation. So the question "what can this key do?" has to be answered by
*capability*, not by asking.

```bash
# every key in Secret Manager, with the tenant each one belongs to
./scripts/probe_klaviyo_key_scopes.sh --all-secrets --control-file <read-only key file>

# a single key, before storing it
./scripts/probe_klaviyo_key_scopes.sh --key-file <file> --control-file <read-only key file>

**It writes nothing.** Klaviyo checks a key's scope *before* it validates the request body, so a
`POST` with an empty body returns `403` when the scope is absent and `400 "Request bodies are
required"` when it is present. Nothing is created either way — safe against live merchant
accounts. Each key also names its own tenant, because `GET /accounts/` returns the organization,
so **no database access is needed** to map keys to tenants.

## Application log files (GH-198)

Every structured event and crash traceback goes to container stdout, which Docker
deletes on any rebuild-class deploy (see the restart-command table above: `--build`
and `--force-recreate` both replace the container). Since GH-198 the Python
processes also write the same JSON lines to a file on the host, which survives all
of it. The file is an additional sink, not a replacement — `docker compose logs`
still shows everything.

now starts with the UTC millisecond prefix (`2026-08-19T18:51:42.380Z `), so a
line is no longer raw JSON on its own. Strip the first space-delimited token
before parsing — `docker compose logs app | cut -d' ' -f2- | jq -R 'fromjson? // empty'`.

### Retention: what prunes what

Three mechanisms, deliberately independent — the first two need nothing running,
which is the point.

* **Size, per file, at write time** — `RotatingFileHandler` in
  `app/observability/logging.py`. Checked on every record rather than on a
  schedule, so a burst of logging cannot outrun it between sweeps.
* **Age, then total size, daily** — `/etc/cron.d/ltvera-log-retention` runs
  `/usr/local/sbin/ltvera-log-retention.sh` as root at 03:15. Deletes anything
  older than 14 days, then oldest-first until the directory is under 2 GiB. It is
  root's cron rather than Celery beat on purpose: beat only runs in production
  (`scripts/start-worker.sh` adds `--beat` when `APP_ENV` is not `local`), and a
  sweep hosted by the worker stops exactly when the worker is wedged.
* **Age, then total size, at process start** — `configure_logging()` runs the same
  policy in Python. This is the whole story in local development, where there is
  no cron and `watchmedo` restarts mint a new PID (and file) on every code edit.

To see what would be deleted without deleting it:

```bash
sudo /usr/local/sbin/ltvera-log-retention.sh --dry-run
```

  sudo docker exec ltvera-pandas-postgres-1 psql -U postgres -d ltvera -c \

### Synthesis model & timeout topology

Answer quality, latency, and the end-to-end timeout budget are governed by the
`synthesis` block in
[`ask_self/ask_self_harness.json`](ask_self/ask_self_harness.json). The agent reads
the harness at startup, so edit the block then `sudo systemctl restart rag-agent-ltvera`:

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `synthesis.model` | `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` | The committed harness is the file `rag-agent.sh` actually reads. Pro-tier synthesis is ~25–35s/query; Sleuth's `REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` (90s) was raised specifically to absorb that. Do not "fix" this table back to `gemini-flash-latest` without changing the harness — Flash was a temporary workaround when the timeout was 30s. |
| `synthesis.max_output_tokens` | `8192` | The ask-self default `1500` truncated longer answers mid-JSON; `synthesize()`'s fallback then dumped a raw, double-encoded JSON blob into the `answer` field. 8192 keeps the response complete and single-encoded. |

**Timeout topology — there is no nginx on this VM.** The path is
Slack → Sleuth → Caddy → rag-agent. The binding timeout is **Sleuth-side**:
`REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` (90s) in `sleuth-app`'s `src/chat-commands/ask-code-command.js`,
not on this VM. Caddy's `/rag-agent/*` route ([`deploy/Caddyfile`](deploy/Caddyfile))
is a bare `reverse_proxy` with **no read timeout**, so the proxy never caps the
response. The Sleuth-side ASKCODE integration doc's advice to raise an nginx
`proxy_read_timeout` does **not** apply here — this deployment fronts the agent with
Caddy, not nginx.

  and confirm `synthesis.model` is `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` in the committed
  harness (then restart the agent if the VM copy drifted). A cold-started agent's
  first query runs slower than steady state.
- **Slack shows a raw or truncated JSON blob** instead of prose — `synthesis.max_output_tokens`

  restart the agent. (A robustness fix for the truncation fallback itself lives in

When an incident here needs a third party to act (NexMail, Klaviyo, Shopify),
the write-up is an **ops deliverable** — and it is short.

- **First line: FYI or ASK**, and the ask itself. If nothing is needed from them,

- **Numbered questions**, nothing between them.
- **Evidence in a `<details>` block or linked to our PROJECT doc** — never the body.

The Dispatch widget opens on **Nexmail** for a tenant with an adopted brand, and on the

What decides it (`resolve_default_draft_provider`, `app/campaigns/wiring.py`):

## Outbound email (Mailgun)

> GH-157. One provider, two paths: **app-originated mail** goes through
> `app/mailer.py` `send_email()` (Mailgun HTTP API); **Keycloak transactional
> mail** (activation, password reset) is sent by Keycloak itself via realm
> SMTP, pointed at Mailgun. Both send from the verified `mg.ltvera.com`
> subdomain — do not move the from-addresses off it (SPF/DKIM alignment under
> the root domain's DMARC policy depends on it).

Two distinct GSM secrets, under **split IAM bindings** — never interchangeable:

| Secret | Consumer | Identity allowed to read |
|---|---|---|
| `ltvera-mailgun-api-key` | `app/mailer.py` (HTTP API) | app/worker runtime SA |
| `ltvera-mailgun-smtp-password` | `configure-smtp` below | operator identity only |

App mail config (worker + any one-shot job): `MAILGUN_API_KEY_SECRET_REF`
points at the API-key secret version; `MAILGUN_DOMAIN` / `MAILGUN_FROM` /
`MAILGUN_REPLY_TO` default to `mg.ltvera.com` / `ops@mg.ltvera.com` /
`devops@binoidcbd.com`. An empty ref hard-fails the send before any network
call — there is no silent no-op.

**Two senders, on purpose.** The two paths use two from-addresses and neither
needs to change:

| Sender | Path | Reply-to | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ops@mg.ltvera.com` | `app/mailer.py` helper | `devops@binoidcbd.com` | Fire-and-forget machine alerts. They go *to* `CONNECTION_HEALTH_OPS_TO` (the same inbox), so a reply-to there keeps the thread in one place — `mg.ltvera.com` has no inbox (GH-167). |
| `devops@mg.ltvera.com` | Keycloak realm SMTP | `devops@ltvera.com` | Human-facing activation / reset mail. A person may reply, so it carries a **root-domain** reply-to — `mg.ltvera.com` has no inbox. |

Both send from the verified `mg.ltvera.com` subdomain for SPF/DKIM alignment;
only the reply-to leaves it, which does not affect alignment. The two reply-tos
differ deliberately: the helper's lands in the ops inbox that received the
alert, the realm's lands on the root-domain mailbox for human-facing mail.

```

It PUTs `smtp.mailgun.org:587` (STARTTLS, user `postmaster@mg.ltvera.com`,
from `devops@mg.ltvera.com`, `replyTo devops@ltvera.com`) and prints the

**root-domain** address on purpose: `mg.ltvera.com` has no inbox, so a reply-to
mirroring the sender would send every reply into the void (see

## VM start failures (capacity stockouts) — GH-207

> **Alarm-only; capacity change deferred (2026-08-27).** Production (`app.ltvera.com`) runs on `c3-standard-4` in `us-central1-a` and stops overnight. Stockouts on instance-schedule start leave the VM off until manually started. Moving to reserved capacity was deferred in favor of a zero-cost alarm.

A Cloud Monitoring alert policy (`ltvera-vm-start-failure`) fires when an instance-schedule start fails due to a zone stockout (`ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED`). It notifies the operator email channel within minutes.

**If the alarm fires:**
1. A zone stockout occurred at the scheduled start time (e.g. 04:00 PT).
2. Manually start the instance: `gcloud compute instances start ltvera-dev --zone us-central1-a`
3. If capacity remains exhausted, you may need to wait or change the machine type/zone as an operator cost decision.

## buffer-server-pg Backups and PITR (GH-115)

Automated backups for the Cloud SQL instance `buffer-server-pg` are enabled with a 7-day retention window. The backup window starts at `07:00` UTC (during the nightly off-hours of the main app VM).

**Open Operator Decision:** Point-in-time recovery (PITR) is currently disabled. Enabling PITR adds continuous WAL/write-storage cost. Since `buffer-server-pg` is the only copy of in-flight events before they hit BigQuery, PITR is plausibly warranted, but the cost call is deferred to the operator.
